title: A Alibi for the Ledger
premise: Orsen Joubert, archivist of Saint-Aubin's Cathedral, catalogues the belongings of Vivienne Marsh, a donor who vanished thirty years ago, and discovers her diary continues writing entries for dates that haven't happened yet. When an entry names Orsen's own death, she begins investigating the night in 1994 when three friends locked the crypt and only two walked out — alibis built on a ledger of debts, forged identities, and an inheritance none of them earned. As Orsen follows the diary's prophecies backward through the cathedral's records, she learns Vivienne never died: she became someone else entirely, hiding inside the very institution Orsen serves. The final entries were written by Vivienne herself, alive and watching, testing whether Orsen will expose the truth or inherit the silence — and Orsen chooses to burn the ledger, freeing them both.
about_author: Gideon Winterbourne is the pen name of a former parish registrar who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed estates before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about paper trails outliving the people who left them.

chapters.title: The Accession Number
chapters.summary: Orsen Joubert, POV. While accessioning the estate of missing donor Vivienne Marsh, Orsen finds her diary among the effects and notices the handwriting continues past the disappearance date. The emotional beat is quiet professional unease curdling into fascination as Orsen realizes the impossible object in her hands.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Orsen, POV. Reading by lamplight, she finds the diary's later entries describe events with unsettling accuracy — including one dated next week naming her. She photographs pages, hides the book, and tells no one. The beat is dread disguised as diligence.

chapters.title: The Locked Crypt
chapters.summary: Orsen, POV. She petitions Dean Halvard to reopen the sealed crypt where Vivienne was last seen in 1994; he refuses, citing canon law. Father Ambrose, the sole surviving witness, deflects her questions with practiced warmth. Beat: first wall, first lie.

chapters.title: Three Who Went Down
chapters.summary: Interleaved 1994 testimony excerpts, documentary POV. Police statements from Ambrose, verger Tomas Reil, and Vivienne's sister Colette each place the others below ground. The accounts align too perfectly. Beat: the reader sees the alibi's seams before Orsen does.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Debts
chapters.summary: Orsen, POV. In the cathedral financial archive she finds a private ledger recording loans between the three witnesses and Vivienne — sums forgiven the week after the disappearance. Beat: motive surfaces; money changed hands over a closed door.

chapters.title: Colette Comes Home
chapters.summary: Colette, POV. Now terminally ill, Colette returns to town and asks Orsen directly whether the diary has surfaced. Her fear isn't grief but exposure. Beat: the antagonist-adjacent figure enters, sympathetic and dangerous.

chapters.title: A Name Not Hers
chapters.summary: Orsen, POV. Following a hunch from the diary's marginalia, Orsen matches Vivienne's handwriting to donation letters signed under another name — a woman who joined the cathedral staff years ago and still works there. Beat: vertigo; the missing person may be present.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Vestry
chapters.summary: Marguerite (the renamed Vivienne), POV. We learn she has lived thirty years as a sacristan, bound by the others' silence and her own guilt over what happened in the crypt — not murder, but something she agreed to bury. Beat: sympathy shifts; everyone is guilty of something smaller than the crime suspected.

chapters.title: What the Diary Predicts
chapters.summary: Orsen, POV. The 'prophecy' entry comes true in small, deniable ways: a fire alarm, a fallen scaffold. Orsen tests the diary against chance and fails to dismiss it. Beat: rationality strains; the mystery tightens around time itself.

chapters.title: Tomas Breaks
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. The aging verger, drinking, nearly confesses to Orsen that the crypt door was locked from outside — by him, on instruction. He stops short, terrified of the ledger's final page. Beat: the alibi structure cracks visibly.

chapters.title: The Final Page
chapters.summary: Orsen, POV. She obtains the ledger's last page: a transfer of the Marsh inheritance to a trust controlled by all three witnesses, contingent on Vivienne remaining legally dead. Beat: the full architecture of the conspiracy revealed — inheritance as ransom for silence.

chapters.title: Threats in the Stacks
chapters.summary: Orsen, POV. Someone searches her office; the diary is gone. A note quotes her own accession notes back at her. Beat: hunter becomes hunted; isolation deepens as colleagues close ranks.

chapters.title: Ambrose's Sermon
chapters.summary: Ambrose, POV. Preaching on forgiveness, he privately rehearses thirty years of complicity, believing he protected the church, not himself. He decides Orsen must be discredited quietly. Beat: institutional evil wearing vestments.

chapters.title: The Second Diary
chapters.summary: Marguerite, POV. Marguerite reveals herself to Orsen in the vestry: she wrote the future-dated entries herself, planting the diary to force someone to finally look. Beat: the supernatural dissolves into desperate human design — and relief.

chapters.title: Why She Stayed Dead
chapters.summary: Marguerite, POV. Vivienne explains: she faked her death to escape Colette's coercive control and the debt trap, then stayed hidden because exposure would void the trust — which funds the cathedral's hospice. Innocents depend on her erasure. Beat: moral weight lands; no clean truth available.

chapters.title: Colette's Bargain
chapters.summary: Colette, POV. Dying, Colette offers Orsen the full confession in exchange for burning the ledger — protecting her children's inheritance. Beat: temptation; the reader feels the pull of the quiet lie.

chapters.title: Night in the Crypt
chapters.summary: Orsen, POV. Lured below with a false message, Orsen is locked in the crypt by Ambrose, who intends an 'accident' echoing 1994. In the dark she finds physical evidence Vivienne left decades ago. Beat: climax begins; history repeating with Orsen in the victim's place.

chapters.title: The Door Opens Both Ways
chapters.summary: Marguerite/Tomas, alternating POV. Marguerite, expecting this move, has armed Tomas with his long-withheld testimony; together they open the crypt and confront Ambrose with the ledger page and his own signature. Beat: the buried testify; the alibi collapses in the room where it was built.

chapters.title: Confession at the Altar Rail
chapters.summary: Ambrose, POV. Broken, Ambrose admits he orchestrated the cover-up to protect the cathedral's endowment, persuading the others the lie was charity. Beat: villainy revealed as self-deception; pity without pardon.

chapters.title: What Orsen Decides
chapters.summary: Orsen, POV. With police involved and Ambrose charged, Orsen holds the ledger and the diary — enough to unravel everything, including the hospice funding and Marguerite's freedom. She weighs exposure against mercy. Beat: the thematic crux made concrete.

chapters.title: Burning the Ledger
chapters.summary: Orsen and Marguerite, alternating POV. Orsen burns the ledger before the trust can be contested, letting the inheritance stand as restitution; Marguerite chooses to remain Marguerite, legally dead but finally free, and gives Orsen the true last entry. Beat: costly grace; identity chosen rather than inherited.

chapters.title: Accession Closed
chapters.summary: Orsen, POV. Months later, Orsen catalogs the case file, writes a neutral finding, and keeps one blank diary page as a bookmark — memory preserved, identity released. The crypt reopens as a memorial. Beat: resolution; the archivist learns some lives are best archived as absence.
